Last year, we made out of this EUR 200 million, this year we are making very little out of this process. Asset quality, we expect, we traditionally were around 4% or 4-something percent in SCUSA. In the cost of risk, less than 5%. Now the cost of risk in US, the whole US, is 1.5%. What the bank is, you split between the bank. The bank is very low cost of risk. It's meaningless.
All the cost of risk you are seeing now, the 1.5% comes from SCUSA, okay? This normalization will happen over time, and it depends not necessarily on the past. As we are generating higher FICO scores, we also expect lower cost of risk when the unemployment deteriorate. I think unemployment continues to be the main driver, not as much as interest rates. Remember that we here are lending a very high yield, and the impact of additional 100 basis points or 50 or 200 basis points in the yield is not meaningful when you are lending at 20% or something like that. Auto to 21 is not as important as it is in the prime space, where the changes in the rates can produce more significant changes in the monthly installments. I think I answer your questions, yeah.
Begoña Morenes
Global Head of Investor Relations, Banco Santander
Thank you, José Antonio, and thank you, Ignacio, for your questions. Can we have the next question, please?
Operator
The next question is coming from Carlos Peixoto from CaixaBank. Please go ahead.
Carlos Peixoto
Senior Director of Equity Research, CaixaBank
Yes. Hi, hi, good morning. A couple of questions from my side as well. I was just wondering, and well, the first one is really just a follow-up, but because I believe I missed exactly the guidance that you had given for NII in Brazil for the full year. On the second question, I was wondering on the outlook for cost of risk in Spain. I believe that in the past you had mentioned something in the areas of 50 basis points. Right now, cost of risk is still trending a bit above those levels. I was wondering how you see it for the second half of the year and possibly to 2023. Thank you.
José Antonio Álvarez
CEO, Banco Santander
NII in Brazil in H2 of the year. A mid-single digit growth in Brazil is what you should expect for NII in Brazil for the whole year. While the cost of risk in Spain hasn't changed our expectations we set 50 to 60 basis points for the whole year. Probably this is what you should expect for Spain this year. While naturally this means, as you know, the cost of risk now largely depends on the macro scenarios? Well, I told you that EUR 600 million in H1 came from the macro. Well, the H2, the macro is so uncertain in these days that well, we will see what kind of macro we introduce at the end of the year.
If the macro remains as it is today, let's take IMF expectations that they published yesterday, day before yesterday, should stay in these levels, yeah. As I said to you before, we do not expect a big deal this year on the ground coming from the cost of risk, yeah.
Begoña Morenes
Global Head of Investor Relations, Banco Santander
Thank you, José Antonio. Thank you, Carlos, for your questions. Can we have the next one, please?
Operator
The next question is coming from Andrea Filtri from Mediobanca. Please go ahead.
Andrea Filtri
Co-Head of Research, Mediobanca
Thank you. Two questions. One on rate sensitivity. This is the flavor of the moment, but the visibility you're giving is still quite low compared to other names. Can you please give us for each main area your 12-month rate sensitivity, assuming zero deposit beta, if you plugged in the forward curve that we can all see, just to add some transparency on that front? I didn't understand quite well before, José Antonio, your elaboration around the reason not to have any Spanish bonds, ALCO portfolio in Spain and how big the ALCO should be in a normalized scenario. The second question is on Brazil, again, on the rate sensitivity.
You elaborated quite a lot around this, but I wanted to understand in Brazilian reais term what you would expect then to be the tailwind on a full phasing when the liability repricing stops and asset repricing at the current rates level is completed to understand the- Does the pendulum swing from the negative headwind to the positive tailwind, and hence, how much can this play in terms of cost of risk? Thank you.
José Antonio Álvarez
CEO, Banco Santander
Okay. Let me elaborate. José will guide you through the specific details on numbers you see. Rates, sensitivity to rates. Yeah, so we're gonna give you an easy representation, the parallel shift on the yield curve, but you ask for areas. High level, I should say that with the forward, normally what happens is this is a process that is accelerating. So if I take the whole 2023 with the forward rates, probably in Europe, we think we should think in all our business in Europe, EUR 2 billion, north of EUR 2 billion, probably. This is a figure that, well, you know, there is plenty of numbers there, but this is a figure that sounds reasonable to me.
You asked for the Spanish ALCO, well, I may in terms of duration, but having an ALCO between EUR 20 and 40 billion is something that sounds to me reasonable to. ALCO does not necessarily mean one single sovereign. Means a portfolio of fixed rate assets that we do not generate in commercial terms. In commercial terms, as you know, the majority of our 80% of the mortgage book, the majority of the lending to SMEs and corporates, and 100% of the lending to CIB or almost 100% of the lending to CIB is floating rate.
On the other way around is a limited asset that we generate a fixed rate, and for that reason, the need of having a significant ALCO portfolio in Spain, and we don't have because our view of our interest rates was that they should go up, and that's the reason why we don't have this portfolio. José, you want to-
José García Cantera
CFO and Senior EVP, Banco Santander
Yeah.
José Antonio Álvarez
CEO, Banco Santander
Clarify the specific data?
José García Cantera
CFO and Senior EVP, Banco Santander
Yeah. The reason we give a parallel shift. Well, parallel shift really is from one day to 12 months. The sensitivity we have doesn't go beyond 12 months, obviously. When we talk about a parallel shift, we are talking about a movement between overnight and 12 months. The reason we give a parallel shift is because today, for instance, the market is expecting rates in Europe to stay at 1%, while just a month ago, it was much higher than that. It's much better to look at sensitivity and then for a parallel shift, which is again a movement between a day and 12 months, and then you put your own, you know, outlook of rates.
For a parallel shift of 100 basis points and a 25% beta, the sensitivity in Spain is EUR 750 million, in the UK is EUR 300 million, most of which we have already seen, by the way. In the UK, we would expect further sensitivity in the H2 of this year, and then probably some stabilization in 2023, EUR 140 million in the US. For the second year, this is relevant for Brazil. In Brazil, in the second year, we would expect a positive sensitivity of around EUR 150 million.
If we are right, and then the last interest rate hike takes place in August, September, and then we start seeing the positive sensitivity flowing through the P&L in Brazil towards the end of this year, beginning of next year, then we should see the sensitivity in the P&L in Brazil, which is around EUR 140 to 150 million. This sensitivity to a parallel shift is in the presentation.
Begoña Morenes
Global Head of Investor Relations, Banco Santander
Thank you, José and José Antonio. Thank you, Andrea, for your question. Can we have the next one, please?
Operator
Just a quick reminder, to ask a question, press star one. The next question is coming from Carlos Cobo Catena from Societe Generale. Please go ahead.
Carlos Cobo Catena
Director of Equity Research, Societe Generale
Hi. Thank you very much for taking my questions. A couple of questions from me. One is on M&A appetite now that you've ruled out Mexico. There's been some reports in the media about you exploring some agreements or expanding the agreements with car makers in Europe. You've always been very interested in your consumer finance business. Could that be an area where you could do some bolt-on deals? How material, if you could quantify that, they might be in terms of capital consumption, if it's possible to give some view. I understand there's been some pop-ups in the macro provisions overlay. Could you elaborate on which countries you've allocated that provision?
Because we've seen how Spanish peers aren't really popping up that COVID overlay. It'll be interesting to see if you differ from them. That's it. That's my two questions. Thank you very much.
José Antonio Álvarez
CEO, Banco Santander
Thank you, Carlos. Well, M&A appetite, we are not looking. What you mentioned is agreement with OEMs. Well, we look at this as almost as a BAU. If I look backwards in the last year, we signed three important deals. The main one was Stellantis. That was a restructuring of the previous deal that will bring to us. Our portfolio as a result of this will grow in the region of EUR 5 billion with an agreement with Stellantis. We reached another important agreement with Mitsubishi to be the provider in the US. We've done another agreement, very important, this one, with Honda in Mexico to be the provider for Honda in Mexico. Naturally, we have plenty of discussions, in some cases for one country, in some cases for the whole Europe.
Probably we have several of those open, but nothing that I can communicate at this stage because. I see this as a BAU for the division of digital consumer finance. Reaching agreements with the OEMs means, in some cases, that we establish a joint venture with them, in which we match the financial side, and they match the commercial side of the joint venture, or having a white label, providing white label to them and provide our services to their. We agree in this. I forgot to mention that we also reached an agreement in Greece last year with the main importer in Greece that has 30% market share.
This is, as I should say, business as usual, and is in our projections that we gave for the business as usual in the Digital Consumer Bank space. The provisions overlay I said before, but well, this EUR 600 million is, roughly speaking, numbers, EUR 100 million in Spain, EUR 260 million in UK, and EUR 130 million in US. Those are the EUR 600 million that you have embedded due to macro in the H1 results.
Begoña Morenes
Global Head of Investor Relations, Banco Santander
Thank you, José Antonio, and thank you, Carlos, for your question. Can we have the last question, please?
Operator
The last question is coming from Britta Schmidt from Autonomous Research. Please go ahead.
Britta Schmidt
Senior Analyst, Autonomous Research
Yeah. Hi there. Good morning. I've got two questions please. One is on the rate outlook for Brazil. The consensus expects that there will be rate cuts in 2023, and maybe you can help us work through the dynamics of your NII outlook then. Could we see even wider spreads, let's say, in the second half of 2023, depending, of course, on the timing? My second question will be on Poland. Do you have any update on the WIBOR issues there? Do you expect this still to become a legal case and drag on? What's the latest from the ground? Thank you.
José Antonio Álvarez
CEO, Banco Santander
In the rate outlook for Brazil, we expect the rates to peak rather sooner than later, but maybe in August, maybe September this year. While, when those rates start to go down, more difficult to say. As you know, in the very short run, the CFO already elaborate on this. Normally, you should expect one, two quarters negative or positive, and afterwards the commercial dynamics prevail. Yeah. Overall, those are the dynamics and what you should expect from NII. This is the outlook for rates in Brazil while still highly uncertain next year. Yeah. Poland, you're asking me if it's a legal case. It's too early to tell.
While we are, naturally, as of today, analyzing the situation. I provide you the impact, assuming a 50% take-up on the mortgage moratoria. This is a significant damage for the system as a whole. While our colleagues, the financial system in Poland, will take a view on this, while this is not an individual case, this is a whole financial community in Poland that should take the appropriate view on this, when we finish to analyze the proposal from the government.
José García Cantera
CFO and Senior EVP, Banco Santander
Yeah. If I may add, in terms of the WIBOR, we just know that there is a proposal to change it, but we don't have the details. It would start next year, but there are no details at all with regards to the change in the WIBOR. It will be very difficult-

Very difficult. Yeah.

To change the index. I don't know if you want to elaborate, but it would go against recommendations for index regulation in Europe, so it would be very difficult to change. We have no news.

The proposal is difficult to execute. As José said, this European regulations prevent to go this way and that's the situation. We do not expect any news soon, yeah, on this. No. Okay.

Ana Patricia Botín
Executive Chairman, Banco Santander
We have laid these foundations to deliver great value to serve a growing customer base, which is up 30 million customers since 2015, increasing profits and improving profitability. Our ROTE is up close to 170 basis points since 2015, and of course, strengthening our capital base in a very significant way, as well as delivering sustainable returns to our shareholders. Just a couple of numbers on this: We have remunerated shareholders with EUR 19 billion since 2015, and our tangible NAV has grown by EUR 12 billion since then. I'm very pleased to report that a strong 2021 takes us very close to meeting our 2019 investor day targets in spite of the pandemic. Actually, in some cases, we're ahead. We will continue to focus on growth, profitability, and strength, including shareholder remuneration.
We are guiding for 2022 a mid-single-digit revenue growth, a cost-to-income ratio close to 45%, and a return on tangible equity above 13%. We're aiming to keep our fully loaded CET1 at around 12%. We're also aiming to maintain the 40% payout in 2022, of which, as we already said, will be 50% share buybacks and the other 50% in cash. I also want to say that longer term, we aspire to increase our total shareholder remuneration beyond 40% to around 50%, again, through share buybacks and growing our cash dividend whilst maintaining a CET1 of 12%. This would, of course, be subject to future corporate and regulatory decisions and approvals. We'll go to the next slide. You've seen a very strong 2021 result.
Our net profit is actually up 25% from 2019, underlying, in a similar percentage, reflecting, as I said, the strength and resilience of our business model. We onboarded 5 million new customers. We are growing revenues by 7% to over EUR 46 billion. We again increased efficiency and reduced the cost of credit. That's down to just 77 basis points and generating a return to shareholders as measured by tangible NAV per share and cash dividend per share of 11%. Importantly, 2021 was a pivotal year for us in terms of capital. We are at the high end of the range, delivering a 12% CET1 fully loaded. Going forward, as I already said, we expect to keep it at these levels of 12%.
You can hear our P&L here. We have been able to recover, actually more than recover, our pre-pandemic levels of customer activity, in terms of the underlying profit before tax. Again, it's a record high of EUR 15.3 billion. Actually, on the quarter, it's the highest underlying in 12 years, and this is up 21%. Our underlying profit of EUR 8.7 billion, that's up 80% versus last year, 23 compared to 19. This reflects optimal cost of risk, but also very strong execution of what I have said many times is a structural change in our business model. Very importantly, as you can see, revenues are growing more than costs with a positive operating leverage. Very strong capital generation in the year and up to CET1 of 12, even though we had significant regulatory headwinds this year.
Even more important is the strong business momentum, and you can see some examples here. We are moving our business model to more fees, diversifying into different sources of revenue linked to our customer focus. These are only some examples. Loans and deposits are growing, mutual funds are growing at 13%. But in the higher return value-added services, which are really what's adding to our profitability, our POS (point of sale) is up 38%, and insurance premiums are up 12%. Our new Buy Now, Pay Later, this is a business we've built on top of our tech stack, Openbank in Germany. It's going across Europe soon. 2 million customers in the first few months. Debt capital markets, M&A up 16%. This is really important for the future, and these are the businesses in which we're investing more heavily.
José Antonio Álvarez will give you details on the regions later. During the year, we also leveraged the diversification and scale of the group. These are two key elements, and we are working more and more on this key strength of our business model. Operational performance is improving across the board: Europe, North America, and South America. Our Digital Consumer Bank, which, as you know, combines our auto and consumer finance and Openbank, is one of our important growth initiatives. In Europe, we are working really hard to transform the business model. Return on tangible assets is close to 10%. As you can see in the slide, our customer focus is also showing up in better NPS across the different countries. The structural changes have led to cost efficiencies of around EUR 200 million.
This is an area we'll continue to focus on next year. In North America, we generated a return on tangible equity of close to 25%. We are also working on a structural basis in the U.S. I'll give you more details later on. We're really trying very hard to leverage the connectivity across the group, our experience in consumer finance in Europe and Latin America, and other global relationships. Corporate and Investment Banking has also made great progress in North America. In Mexico, we are increasing profitability and being very successful in growing new business, like the auto business organically. South America, again, is a standout performer, with Chile and Brazil being the best banks in terms of profitability in their respective markets, and overall returns of 26%.
We're growing double-digit in terms of revenues, growing in terms of market share, and growing customers in very different segments in all these markets. Our Digital Consumer Bank had another very strong year, producing a return on tangible equity of around 15%. I would like to point to two key numbers in this slide. If you look at the group's customer loans and group underlying profit, you can see Europe is where we have 60% of our loans and 28% of our profits. Again, this means our business is more dependent on lending in Europe. This is something we're working on to increase fees and increase profitability. It also means reduced risk, as a lot of these loans are secured, such as mortgages in countries like the UK and Spain.
In South America, you can see 14% customer loans and 31% underlying profit. This is exactly an example of very positive operating leverage, very diversified businesses, many of them high-growth fee businesses linked to digital initiatives like, you know, auto platforms, Getnet, and other such businesses. The same applies to North America. As you can see, 14% of the loans and 29% of the profits. We have been leading and intend to continue to lead in responsible banking, and here we have very specific targets in terms of our green transition for us and our customers, building a more inclusive society, and of course, talent and diversity. In terms of the green transition, we are working with our customers to help them with that transition. We are focused on delivering on our own net-zero ambition by 2050, which of course includes our customers.
In terms of our own operations, we are already net zero. We are working, again, on the advisory side, on the capital market, but also increasingly developing retail and SME products. We originated EUR 61 billion in green finance in 2019. We have EUR 27 billion under management, and we're the number one bank in project finance in renewable energy. We are, again, making a lot of progress in our very important goal of empowering 10 million individuals by 2025. We're on target to reach that. We've empowered 7 million people in 2019, and also allocated EUR 500 million in microfinance in 2021. As I said before, we are very, very focused and proud to have been the number one bank in the Bloomberg Gender-Equality Index and the number two company worldwide.
This is an area where we'll continue to focus, as we think diversity is not just the right thing; it's also good for business. In summary, responsible banking, we believe, is key to delivering on all our other commitments. We are creating value for our shareholders. We did set a 40% payout of underlying earnings, split in equal parts between cash dividends and also buyback programs. We will be announcing in a couple of weeks the second dividend after the interim dividend of 1.7 EUR, which was half and half between cash and buybacks. We continue to believe buybacks are an excellent investment of our capital, and so that would be the intention for the second dividend as well.
I will now pass over to José Antonio, who's going to review the returns and detailed operating metrics for the year.
José Antonio Álvarez
Spanish banker and former CEO, Banco Santander
Thank you, Ana, and good morning to everyone. As Ana has already commented, we recorded a pretty strong set of results in 2021, with an underlying profit of EUR 8.7 billion, 78% higher year-on-year in constant euros, driven by a very positive performance across the board, notably in the US, UK, Brazil, and the CIB and wealth management businesses. Our net banking income pre-provision profit was around EUR 25 billion, with an increase of 9% year-on-year, which I think is remarkable. This was driven by 7% revenue growth.
Net interest income grew 7% on the back of higher volumes, lower cost of funds, better credit spreads in Latin America, and some positive impact from recent interest rate hikes in some Latin American countries and Poland. Net interest income rose 8% year over year. Double-digit growth occurred in corporates, wholesale banking, and wealth management and insurance due to greater commercial and financial activity. Costs increased at half the pace of the revenue, which has driven significant efficiency improvements. The significant fall in loan loss provision across the group accelerated in Q4, driven by the improvement in the macroeconomic outlook and the very positive performance of our main portfolios.
If we look one step down in the P&L and analyze the quarterly trends in core lines, we saw improving trends across the board on the P&L lines through the year. Q4 was the most profitable quarter of 2021, at EUR 2.3 billion, following a good performance, particularly on the provisioning side. Also, some of the releases were offset by the contribution to the deposit guarantee fund bank levy and the charge for the Swiss francs in Poland. Net-net, the quarter is fairly comparable with the previous ones. In more detail, sustained customer revenue growth, +4% NII, and 3% fee income quarter on quarter, driven by greater volumes, initial impact from interest rate hikes, as I mentioned before, and growth in higher value-added products and services.
Q-on-Q increases in costs are almost fully explained by boundary adjustments, so this does not represent a running rate for the coming year. In addition, a lower loan loss provision in Q4 favored the aforementioned provision release. I will run through the costs and provisions in more detail in the following slides. On the cost side, we have seen significant inflationary pressure around the world. Group costs rose 4% in constant EUR, but were 2% lower in real terms, absorbing higher IT expenses, digital developments, increased activity, and labor agreements that particularly affected the second part of the year. Our efficiency ratio improved to circa 46%. This was basically driven by Europe, minus 5 full percentage points, which has recorded the highest efficiency gains.
I should stress that the cost in Spain went down 7%, in Portugal 5%, and the UK also decreased. There is more to come in 2022, and our running rate will decrease in line with our targets for the region. We continue to make structural changes to our operating model to drive new improvements in productivity, which should enable us to maintain cost growth below inflation and further improve our efficiency rate. On credit quality, the balance sheet remains, I would say, robust. The NPL ratio is 3.16, below 2020 and 2019. Provisions are down 37% in constant EUR, partly due to the releasing of provisions in Q4.
We also significantly reduced the cost of credit, as Ana already mentioned, to 7 basis points below 2020 and 2019 levels, exceeding our initial 2021 target. In 2022, we expect to maintain the cost of credit below our through-the-cycle ratio. Spain will be key as we expect its cost of credit to reduce to approximately 50 basis points, offsetting some normalization in the US and UK. Finally, regarding capital, in 2021, we reached a fully loaded core equity of 11.21%, thanks to the strong operating results we delivered quarter on quarter. In Q4, we generated 42 basis points organically, a combination of net profit, net of dividends, and efficient risk-weighted asset management, as the risk-weighted assets were flat in the quarter.
Negative impacts in the quarter of 2 basis points due to small regulatory impacts. We already spoke about this in the previous quarter. Nine basis points due to market movements affecting some ALCO portfolios, and 5 basis points from the minority interest that's in Mexico. If we include the acquisition of Exclusa that was approved the same week, and was executed the same week, as of 8 basis points, we closed on 31 January 2022, and the announced acquisition of the broker-dealer, Amherst Pierpont, that affects 8 basis points, with this still subject to completion, which will have an impact of 16 basis points on our pro forma CET1 ratio, which will stand at 11.96%. We were able to combine this performance with an increase in the tangible net asset value per share.
Looking at the regions, starting with Europe, we are accelerating our business transformation. This is where we are pushing harder to change our operating model. Profits doubled in the region, reaching EUR 3 billion, with higher profitability due to volume growth, particularly in mortgages, in line with economic recovery. Net operating income was up 24%, supported by wider spreads in most countries. Revenue was up 11%, particularly customer revenue, while costs remained flat due to ongoing efficiency gains. There was a 32% reduction in loan loss provision, and our cost of credit improved to under 40 basis points.
In the following slides, for the sake of clarity, I include the ROTE adjusted to 12% CET1 in all units. We are making this adjustment to allow for a like-for-like comparison between the units, given their very different capital ratios. In Europe, starting with Spain, Spain showed a strong pickup in activity in individuals, mortgages, and consumer lending. Customer funds also grew significantly last year. Profit nearly doubled, boosted by strong net operating income performance. Jaws were 10 percentage points, revenue grew 13%, costs grew 3%, and efficiency gains drove a 7% reduction in cost. Loan loss provisions reduced 8% year on year, and in 2022, we expect to have our cost of credit.
We also expect single-digit balance sheet growth in 2022. In the UK, we improved four-fold. It's a four-fold increase in profit, basically by record net mortgage lending. You don't see this in the loan book that only grows 0.5% due to the fact that we completed the transfer of the CIB business to the London branch, and this affects some of the loan portfolio that went from a ring-fenced bank to the London branch. Plus 22% year-on-year growth in NII due to deposit repricing and volumes on the mortgage that I mentioned before. Cost savings from our transformation program were partially offset by IT investments and regulatory-related programs. Efficiency improved by nearly 11 percentage points. Loan loss provision releases reflecting balance sheet strength. As a result, we achieved double-digit return on tangible equity in the UK.
In North America, we improved our competitive position by increasing connectivity in the region, consolidating IT functions, and advancing significantly in business simplification. We also announced several transactions in 2021, in line with our strategy to deploy capital in the most profitable businesses. Volumes grew, driven by our main segments in both countries. Profit doubled, driven largely by lower provisions and higher revenue in the US. In the US, we had an extremely positive 2021. On a like-for-like basis, excluding Puerto Rico and Bluestem portfolio disposals, loans grew with double-digit growth in auto originations. Customer funds increased due to retail deposits with a significantly lower cost of funding. Underlying profit increased sharply, supported by an 11% increase in net operating income (NII), fees, and auto lease results, and an 85% decline in loan loss provisions.
In short, strong performance, with the US being one of the engines of the group in 2021 results. In Mexico, we increased our stake to over 96% and continue to invest in the franchise, reflecting positive results and customer growth. In a challenging environment, with rate cuts in 2020 and falling volumes, we were able to quickly adapt, resulting in improving trends within the year. As a result, we delivered an 8% increase in profit, thanks to loan and deposit growth, controlled costs well below inflation despite IT investments, and a better cost of credit. Finally, regarding the last region, South America, we continue to strengthen connectivity. We are a market leader across the region. We are capturing synergies across the region and new business opportunities, and boosting our already profitable franchise.
We show strong customer growth in all the countries where we are leaders in quality of service, as measured by NPS. In terms of results in 2021, we delivered greater volumes in all countries, double-digit customer revenue growth, increased productivity with costs growing well below inflation, and a lower cost of credit in all countries. This resulted in strong profit and a very high return on tangible equity. In Brazil, it was another excellent year. Record customer attraction, with more than 5 million customers, translated into significant growth in individuals, loans to individuals growing 22%, consumer finance 12%, and SMEs +15%. This translated into the P&L with a return on tangible equity well above 20%. Double-digit growth in customer revenue and record annual efficiency levels below 30% for the first time. We maintained credit quality at comfortable levels.
In Chile, our digitization process allowed us to significantly increase our customer attraction, which is reflected in the +23% increase in demand deposits and double-digit fee income growth, widening the gap in NPS with our competitors, making us the market leader. We had excellent year-on-year profit performance. NII +10%, improved efficiency, an increasing gap to peers, and a lower cost of credit driven by better-than-expected performance in SMEs and corporates. The consumer bank, the Digital Consumer Bank, had solid balance sheet dynamics. New business activity has recovered to pre-COVID levels, up 10%, despite the challenges posed by COVID restrictions and the semiconductor shortage. Of note was auto, with +13% origination on the back of increasing our market share by 50 basis points across Europe.
Additionally, we are working on the expansion of Openbank, which performed very well in terms of customer increase and volumes this year. Loans grew 48%, and customer funds grew 24%. Total Digital Consumer Bank revenue was boosted by the new business recovery, particularly in consumer leasing. It was a positive year in credit quality, with a further reduction in the cost of credit. In summary, excellent results reflected a 16% underlying profit growth and an increase in profitability return on tangible equity, sitting at 14%. Going to the two businesses we report as secondary segments, both have had a very good year in the industry. For corporate investment banking, revenues grew 10%, a sharp improvement in loan loss provision. We are gaining share, and we are at the top of the market in private finance, top three in private finance in Europe and Latin America.
As Ana mentioned, we are focused on sustainable alternatives and ESG through green financing. We are investing in the business. The cost increased as we are investing in continental Europe, the UK, and the US to develop new capabilities to serve our customers. In wealth management insurance, we saw excellent business performance in 2021. Record commercial flows of EUR 20 billion, with EUR 12 billion in private banking and EUR 8 billion in asset management. Insurance premiums for the protection business increased at double-digit rates. Wealth management insurance's total contribution to the group increased 12% to EUR 2.3 billion.
